claim: The ability to associate sensory stimuli with abstract classes is critical for survival.
source: The ability to associate sensory stimuli with abstract classes is critical for survival.
evidence: This is a general statement drawing from established understanding in neuroscience and evolutionary biology about the importance of categorization for survival.

claim: Experiments have probed two kinds of associations between stimuli and categories: fixed associations and flexible ones.
source: Such experiments have probed two kinds of associations between stimuli and categories: fixed associations (Freedman and Assad, 2006; Fitzgerald et al., 2011; Cromer et al., 2010) (in which, e.g., stimuli are either in category A or in category B), and flexible ones (Wallis et al., 2001; Stoet and Snyder, 2004; Roy et al., 2010; Reinert et al., 2021) (in which, e.g., stimuli are in category A in one context and category B in another).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to experimental studies that investigated these two types of associations.

claim: Activity of single neurons in associative cortex develops selectivity to task-relevant abstract variables such as category and context during learning.
source: A consistent finding in these experiments is that activity of single neurons in associative cortex develops selectivity to task-relevant abstract variables, such as category (Freedman et al., 2001; Fitzgerald et al., 2011; Reinert et al., 2021) and context (White and Wise, 1999; Wallis et al., 2001; Stoet and Snyder, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple experimental studies showing selectivity development.

claim: Neurons in visual cortex encode simple sensory variables via negatively correlated responses.
source: Classical work indicates that neurons in visual cortex encode simple sensory variables (e.g., two opposite orientations) via negatively correlated responses (Hubel and Wiesel, 1962; Olshausen and Field, 2004): neurons that respond strongly to a given variable respond weakly to the other one, and vice versa.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to classical studies in visual cortex.

claim: Responses in visual cortex to different sensory variables are symmetric.
source: Those responses, furthermore, are symmetric (DeAngelis and Uka, 2003): about the same number of neurons respond strongly to one variable, or the other.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to experimental work.

claim: Evidence for negatively correlated and symmetric responses to abstract variables has been reported in monkeys and mice prefrontal cortex.
source: Evidence in favour of this type of responses has been reported in monkeys (White and Wise, 1999; Cromer et al., 2010; Roy et al., 2010; Freedman and Miller, 2008) and mice (Reinert et al., 2021) prefrontal cortex (PFC).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to experimental studies in PFC.

claim: Responses to categories A and B in monkey lateral intraparietal cortex were found to be positively correlated and strongly asymmetric.
source: However, evidence in favour of a different type of responses has been reported in a different set of experiments from monkeys lateral intraparietal (LIP) cortex (Fitzgerald et al., 2013). In that case, responses to categories A and B were found to be positively correlated: neurons that learn to respond strongly to category A also respond strongly to category B, and neurons that learn to respond weakly to category A also respond weakly to category B. Furthermore, responses were strongly asymmetric: almost all neurons displayed the strongest response to the same category (despite monkeys did not display behavioural biases towards one category or the other).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to experimental work in LIP cortex.

claim: The model hypothesizes that synaptic connectivity in neural circuits evolves by implementing gradient descent on an error function.
source: To this end, we hypothesize that synaptic connectivity in neural circuits evolves by implementing gradient descent on an error function (Richards et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a hypothesis stated by the authors as the basis for their model, with citation to related work.

claim: Under gradient-descent plasticity, neural networks can achieve high performance on both simple and complex tasks.
source: A large body of work has demonstrated that, under gradient-descent plasticity, neural networks can achieve high performance on both simple and complex tasks (LeCun et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to machine learning literature.

claim: Gradient-descent learning can be implemented in a biologically plausible way.
source: Recent studies have furthermore shown that gradient-descent learning can be implemented, at least approximately, in a biologically plausible way (Lillicrap et al., 2016; Whittington and Bogacz, 2017; Sacramento et al., 2018; Akrout et al., 2019; Payeur et al., 2021; Pogodin and Latham, 2020; Boopathy and Fiete, 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to recent theoretical studies.

claim: The model can capture experimental findings showing that neurons become selective to category and context after learning.
source: Via mathematical analysis and simulations, we show that the model can capture the experimental findings discussed above. In particular, after learning, neurons in the model become selective to category and, if present, context; this result is robust, and independent of the details of the circuit and the task.
evidence: This claim is supported by the authors' mathematical analysis and simulations presented in the manuscript.

claim: Whether correlations after learning are positive or negative depends on circuit and task details.
source: On the other hand, whether correlations after learning are positive or negative, and whether population tuning to different categories is asymmetric or not, is not uniquely determined, but depends on details.
evidence: This claim is supported by the authors' analysis showing parameter dependence.

claim: Activity measures in the model are modulated by circuit details including activation function, learning rates, and initial connectivity.
source: We determined how, in the model, activity measures are modulated by circuit details (activation function of single neurons, learning rates, initial connectivity) and task features (number of stimuli, and whether or not the associations are context dependent).
evidence: This claim is supported by the authors' systematic analysis of parameter effects.

claim: The circuit model consists of a sensory input layer, an intermediate layer, and a readout neuron.
source: The circuit consists of a sensory input layer (), an intermediate layer (x), and a readout neuron (y). The intermediate (z) and readout (u) weights evolve under gradient descent plasticity (wEquation 1).
evidence: This is a description of the model architecture shown in Figure 1B.

claim: In the simple categorization task, half the stimuli are associated with category A and the other half with category B.
source: In the simple categorization task, half the stimuli are associated with category A and the other half with B.
evidence: This is a description of the task structure shown in Figure 1A.

claim: In the context-dependent task, associations are reversed across contexts.
source: In the context-dependent task, associations are reversed across contexts: stimuli associated with category A in context 1 are associated with category B in context 2, and vice versa.
evidence: This is a description of the task structure shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Before learning, the category selectivity index is zero on average.
source: Before learning, the responses of single neurons to different stimuli are random and unstructured. Thus, responses to stimuli paired with category A are statistically indistinguishable from responses to stimuli paired with category B (Figure 2A). This makes the category selectivity index zero on average (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 2A and 2B.

claim: After learning, the category selectivity index for most neurons increases.
source: After learning, the responses of single neurons depend on category: within-category responses become more similar than across-category responses, resulting in two separate distributions (Figure 2E). As a consequence, the category selectivity index for most neuron increases; correspondingly, average selectivity increases from zero to positive values (Figure 2F), thus reproducing the behaviour observed in experimental studies (Freedman et al., 2001; Freedman and Assad, 2006; Reinert et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 2E and 2F, and is consistent with cited experimental studies.

claim: The selectivity increase is a universal property observed in all circuit models that successfully learned the task, independent of parameters.
source: To determine whether this effect is robust, we varied the parameters that describe the task (number of stimuli) and the biophysical properties of the circuit (the threshold and gain of neurons, Figure 1C, and the learning rates of the two sets of synaptic weights, ηu and ηw). We found that the selectivity increase is a universal property – it is observed in all circuit models that successfully learned the task, independent of the parameters.
evidence: This claim is supported by systematic parameter variation in simulations.

claim: Before learning, activity in response to different stimuli is uncorrelated.
source: As discussed above, before learning the responses of neurons in the intermediate layer are random and unstructured. Thus, activity in response to different stimuli is uncorrelated; this is illustrated in Figure 2C, where all non-diagonal entries of the correlation matrix are close to zero.
evidence: This claim is supported by the correlation matrix shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Over learning, the correlation matrices develop category-dependent structure.
source: Over learning, the correlation matrices develop structure. Correlations become different within the two diagonal, and the two off-diagonal blocks, indicating that learning induces category-dependent structure.
evidence: This claim is supported by the correlation matrices shown in Figure 2G and 2K.

claim: The model can produce both negative and positive category correlations depending on model details.
source: In Figure 2G, the average correlation within the off-diagonal blocks is negative; the category correlation is thus negative (Cromer et al., 2010; Roy et al., 2010; Freedman and Miller, 2008). The model does not, however, always produce negative correlation: varying model details – either the parameters of the circuit or the number of stimuli – can switch the category correlation from negative to positive (Fitzgerald et al., 2013; one example is shown in Figure 2K).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 2G and 2K, and is consistent with cited experimental studies.

claim: When category correlation is negative, changes in single-neuron responses to categories A and B have opposite sign.
source: In Figure 2H, where the category correlation is negative, the cloud has a negative slope. This is because changes in single-neuron responses to categories A and B have opposite sign: a neuron that increases its activity in response to category A decreases its activity in response to category B (Figure 2E left), and vice versa (Figure 2E right).
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis of Figure 2H and 2E.

claim: When category correlation is positive, changes in single-neuron responses to categories A and B have the same sign.
source: In Figure 2L, where the category correlation is positive, the cloud has, instead, a positive slope. Here, changes in single-neuron responses to categories A and B have the same sign: a neuron that increases its activity in response to category A also increases its activity in response to category B (Figure 2I, left), and similarly for a decrease (Figure 2I, right).
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis of Figure 2L and 2I.

claim: Over learning, all activity vectors acquire a component aligned with a common, stimulus-independent direction.
source: Over learning, activity vectors in Figure 3A move. Specifically, over learning all activity vectors acquire a component that is aligned with a common, stimulus-independent direction. Activity after learning can thus be approximated by ys≃y0s+csd where y0s indicates initial activity in response to sensory input s, and d indicates the common direction along which activity acquires structure.
evidence: This claim is supported by mathematical analysis and illustrated in Figure 3.

claim: The coefficients cs are determined by category: approximately equal to cA for category A and cB for category B.
source: The coefficients cs, which measure the strength of the components along the common direction d, are determined by category: they are approximately equal to cA if the sensory input is associated with category A, and cB otherwise.
evidence: This claim is derived from the mathematical analysis of the model.

claim: Activity forms two distinct clouds over learning, one for each category.
source: Consequently, over learning, activity vectors associated with different categories are pushed apart along d; this is illustrated in Figure 3B, C, which show activity for the two circuits analyzed in the second and third column of Figure 2, respectively. Activity thus forms two distinct clouds, one for each category; the centers of the two clouds along d are given, approximately, by cA and cB.
evidence: This claim is supported by the geometric analysis illustrated in Figure 3B and 3C.

claim: The increase in category selectivity is a robust byproduct of gradient-descent learning.
source: The generality of Equation 4 indicates that the increase in selectivity is a robust byproduct of gradient-descent learning, and so can be observed in any circuit that learns the categorization task, regardless of model details.
evidence: This claim is derived from the mathematical analysis showing the generality of the result.

claim: Category correlation depends on the threshold and gain of the readout neuron.
source: In Figure 4A, we show category correlation as a function of the threshold and gain of the readout neuron (Figure 1C). We find that varying those can change the magnitude and sign of correlations, with positive correlations favoured by large values of the threshold and gain and negative correlations favoured by small values.
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Category correlation is affected by the threshold and gain of neurons in the intermediate layer.
source: Category correlation is also affected by the threshold and gain of neurons in the intermediate layer. This can be seen in Figure 4B, which shows that larger values of the threshold and gain tend to favour positive correlation.
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Increasing the ratio of learning rates ηw/ηu causes category correlation to decrease.
source: An equally important role is played by the relative learning rates of the the readout, w, and the intermediate weights, u. As illustrated in Figure 4C, increasing the ratio of the learning rates, ηw/ηu, causes the correlation to decrease.
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Increasing the number of stimuli causes a systematic decrease in category correlation.
source: Category correlation also depends on the total number of stimuli, a property of the task rather than the circuit (Materials and methods Simple task: category correlation, Equation 77). This is illustrated in Figure 4D, which shows that increasing the number of stimuli causes a systematic decrease in correlation.
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The model predicts that increasing the number of stimuli should push category correlation from positive to negative values.
source: The model thus makes the experimentally testable prediction that increasing the number of stimuli should push category correlation from positive to negative values.
evidence: This is a prediction derived from the model's behavior with respect to stimulus number.

claim: Only neurons that are initially strongly connected to the readout neuron exhibit a large selectivity index.
source: Mathematical analysis (see Materials and methods Simple task: computing activity, especially Equation 55) indicates that, for the current task, the category direction d is approximately aligned with the vector that specifies connectivity between the intermediate and the readout neurons, w, before learning starts; we denote this vector w0 (Figure 3B, C). As a consequence, only neurons that are initially strongly connected to the readout neuron – that is, neurons for which w0,i is large – exhibit a large selectivity index (Figure 5B, C).
evidence: This claim is supported by mathematical analysis and simulation results shown in Figure 5B and 5C.

claim: The learning algorithm is characterized by inertia, relying on initial connectivity structure more than learned changes.
source: The fact that activity changes are mostly aligned with w0 indicates that the learning algorithm is characterized by a sort of inertia, which makes it rely on initial connectivity structure much more heavily than on the learned one.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the mathematical analysis results.

claim: Changes in selectivity are determined by the strength of synaptic connections a neuron makes to downstream readout areas before learning.
source: In terms of biological circuits, Figure 5 predicts that changes in selectivity are determined by the strength of synaptic connections a neuron makes, before learning, to downstream readout areas.
evidence: This is a prediction derived from the model analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: Experiments in rodents PFC found that neurons highly selective to an abstract variable projected to the same downstream area.
source: Experiments consistent with this prediction have been recently reported: studies in rodents PFC (Ye et al., 2016; Hirokawa et al., 2019) found that all neurons which were highly selective to a given abstract variable were characterized by similar downstream projections (i.e., they projected to the same area).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: In the context-dependent task, average category selectivity increases over learning.
source: Before learning, activity is characterized by small selectivity, which is weakly negative on average (Figure 6A; the fact that average category selectivity is initially weakly negative is due to the composite nature of inputs for this task, see Materials and methods Detailed analysis of category selectivity). Over learning, the average category selectivity increases (Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 6A and 6D.

claim: The increase in category selectivity in the context-dependent task is highly robust and does not depend on model details.
source: We tested the robustness of this behaviour by varying the parameters that control both the circuit (threshold and gain of neurons, learning rates) and task (number of stimuli and context cues). As in the simple task, we found that the average category selectivity increases in all circuit models, regardless of the parameters (Figure 6G and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by systematic parameter variation in simulations.

claim: Average context selectivity increases over learning in the context-dependent task.
source: For this we measure context selectivity which, analogously to category selectivity, quantifies the extent to which single-neuron activity is more similar within than across contexts (Materials and methods Context-dependent task: category and context selectivity, Equation 122). Context selectivity is shown in Figure 6B, E. We find, as we did for category selectivity, that average context selectivity increases over learning – a behaviour that is in agreement with experimental findings (Wallis et al., 2001; Stoet and Snyder, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 6B and 6E, and is consistent with cited experimental studies.

claim: The increase in context selectivity is highly robust and does not depend on model details.
source: The increase in context selectivity is, as for category, highly robust, and does not depend on model details (Figure 6H and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by systematic parameter variation in simulations.

claim: Context correlation can either decrease or increase over learning depending on circuit parameters.
source: To quantify this, we focus on the off-diagonal blocks (pairs of trials from different contexts) and measure the average of those correlations, which we refer to as context correlation. Context correlation behaves differently in the two circuits displayed in Figure 6F and I: it decreases over learning in Figure 6F, whereas it increases in Figure 6I.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 6F and 6I.

claim: In the context-dependent task, activity forms four clouds, one for each combination of category and context.
source: As in the simple task (Figure 3B, C), activity vectors get re-arranged into statistically distinguishable clouds. While in the simple task clouds were determined by category, here each cloud is associated with a combination of category and context. As a result, four clouds are formed: the cloud of orange circles corresponds to category A and context 1; orange squares to category A and context 2; blue circles to category B and context 1; and blue squares to category B and context 2.
evidence: This claim is supported by the geometric analysis illustrated in Figure 7B and 7C.

claim: Activity clustering occurs along two directions: one for category (dcat) and one for context (dctx).
source: The transition from unstructured activity (Figure 7A) to four clouds of activity (Figure 7B, C) occurs by learning-induced movement along two directions: dcat, which corresponds to category, and dctx, which corresponds to context.
evidence: This claim is supported by the geometric analysis illustrated in Figure 7.

claim: The emergence of context-related structure is a signature of the gradient-descent learning rule.
source: The emergence of context-related structure is, on the other hand, more surprising, since the activity of the readout neuron does not depend on context. Nevertheless, context-dependent structure, in the form of clustering, emerges in the intermediate layer activity. Such novel structure is a signature of the gradient-descent learning rule used by the circuit (Canatar et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by the authors' analysis and citation to related work.

claim: Context clustering emerges because how similarly intermediate-layer representations evolve is determined by both target category and correlations.
source: But, roughly speaking, context clustering emerges because, for a pair of sensory inputs, how similarly their intermediate-layer representations evolve during learning is determined both by their target category and their correlations (Equation 27, Materials and methods Evolution of connectivity and activity in large circuits).
evidence: This claim is derived from the mathematical analysis of the model.

claim: Context correlation depends on the threshold and gain of neurons, relative learning rate, and number of stimuli.
source: In Figure 7D–F, we show how context correlation depends on model parameters. This dependence is qualitatively similar to that of category correlation in the simple task: context correlation depends on the threshold and gain of neurons (compare Figure 7D and Figure 4A), on the relative learning rate ηw/ηu (compare Figure 7E and Figure 4C), and on the number of stimuli (compare Figure 7F and Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 7D-F.

claim: The parameter region leading to increased correlation shrinks substantially in the context-dependent task compared to the simple task.
source: However, we find that the region of parameter space leading to an increase in correlation shrinks substantially compared to the simple task (Figure 6—figure supplement 2C, see also Materials and methods Context-dependent task: computing activity); this is in line with the observation that correlations decrease to negative values when the complexity of the task increases, as shown in Figure 4D.
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Both category and context directions (dcat and dctx) are strongly correlated with the initial readout vector w0.
source: Analysis in Materials and methods Analysis of patterns of context and category selectivity shows that both the category and context directions, dcat and dctx, are strongly correlated with the initial readout vector w0.
evidence: This claim is derived from the mathematical analysis.

claim: Neurons that strongly increase selectivity to either category or context are strongly connected to the downstream readout neuron before learning.
source: As in the simple task, this leads to the prediction that neurons that strongly increase selectivity to either category or context are, before learning, strongly connected to the downstream readout neuron (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is a prediction derived from the model analysis and shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Among strongly selective neurons, some develop mixed selectivity to category and context, others develop pure selectivity to category, but none develop pure selectivity to context.
source: In Figure 8B, we plot changes in context selectivity as a function of changes in category selectivity. We observe that, among all the neurons that strongly increase their selectivity, some increase selectivity to both category and context (orange sample neuron), and others increase selectivity to category, but not context (yellow sample neuron). In contrast, none increases selectivity to context but not category.
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 8B.

claim: The model predicts that neurons with pure selectivity to category and mixed selectivity to category and context should be observed, but neurons with pure selectivity to context should not.
source: This makes the following experimental prediction: among all the neurons that are strongly connected to the readout, neurons with pure selectivity to category and neurons with mixed selectivity to category and context should be observed, but neurons with pure selectivity to context should not.
evidence: This is a prediction derived from the model analysis.

claim: The asymmetry between category and context arises because the readout neuron learns to read out category but not context.
source: The asymmetry between category and context arises because, in the model, the readout neuron learns to read out category, but not context.
evidence: This is an explanation derived from the model structure.

claim: When a second readout neuron that learns to read out context is included, neurons with strong pure selectivity to context are also observed.
source: We show in Figure 6—figure supplement 3E, F that if a second readout neuron, which learns to read out context, is included in the circuit, neurons with strong pure selectivity to context are also observed.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3E, F.

claim: Pure- and mixed-selective neurons are characterized by different patterns of initial response gain.
source: Analysis reported in Materials and methods Analysis of patterns of context and category selectivity indicates that these two populations are characterized by different properties of the initial activity. In particular, the two populations are characterized by different initial patterns of the response gain (defined as the slope of the activation function, Figure 1C, at the response), which measures the local sensitivity of neurons to their inputs.
evidence: This claim is derived from the mathematical analysis and illustrated in Figure 8C.

claim: Initial activity plays an important role in learning by breaking symmetry among neurons and determining functional specialization.
source: Overall, these results indicate that initial activity, which is mostly unstructured and task-agnostic, plays an important role in learning: it breaks the symmetry among neurons in the intermediate layer, and determines which functional specialization neurons will display over learning.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the analysis of how initial conditions affect learning outcomes.

claim: The model provides a framework for interpreting seemingly disparate experimental findings.
source: Overall, the model provides a framework for interpreting seemingly disparate experimental findings, and for making novel experimental predictions.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the contribution of the work.

claim: The model can recapitulate experimental observations including seemingly disparate ones.
source: We find that the model is able to recapitulate experimental observations, including seemingly disparate ones.
evidence: This is a summary of the model's capabilities based on the analyses presented.

claim: The dependencies of activity measures on circuit and task details make experimentally testable predictions.
source: These dependencies make experimentally testable predictions about the circuitry supporting abstract knowledge acquisition in the brain.
evidence: This is a statement about the predictive value of the model.
